claims.text: A combined DSC–dilatometry protocol can accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting across representative single-phase HEAs.
Single-phase HEAs spanning FCC, BCC, and HCP structures are representative candidate materials for the protocol.
Al0.5CoCrFeNi is a suitable example representing FCC/BCC phases.
Temperature ramps of 5–20 K/min under inert gas, extending just beyond the solidus, are appropriate for the combined protocol.
HEA thermal measurements can be performed under nitrogen or argon atmospheres.
Temperature and enthalpy calibration with standard reference materials is applicable to DSC measurements of HEAs.
The controlled inert atmosphere ensures minimal oxidation and measurement interference throughout the proposed near-melting measurements.
The onset of melting is identifiable from endothermic peaks in the DSC heat-flow curve.
Simultaneous dilatometry records volume expansion associated with fusion.
Integration of the DSC melting signal directly yields the latent heat and enthalpy of fusion.
Baseline subtraction using heat-capacity data permits determination of entropy of fusion.
The dilatometric volume-change signal provides an independent confirmation of the DSC melting event.
Melting temperatures can be determined with ±1–2% accuracy.
Enthalpy and derived entropy of fusion can be determined within ±5% uncertainty.
Dilatometric volume-change data will correlate with microscopic structural changes observed by complementary imaging.
Calibration with standard metals and previously characterized HEAs establishes a reliable baseline for both DSC and dilatometry.
The protocol is principally applicable to single-phase HEAs because overlapping transitions in multiphase materials can distort the DSC baseline and reduce accuracy.
Baseline-subtraction difficulties and minor reversible or nanoscale transitions near melting can add measurement variance.
Independent fusion-property measurements and measurements across multiple heating rates can be used to validate the integrated protocol.

The approach is falsified if melting temperatures differ from benchmarks by more than 2%, enthalpy or entropy uncertainty exceeds 5%, or the volume-change signal fails to correlate with the DSC melting onset.
